header.title: Lindsey Mertz · Upside
header.sub: Hiring-manager call Tue Oct 20 (closed, promising). Next: recruiter Katie, then senior engineer, vibe-coding, system design, CIO and Deputy CIO.

p: Get past the engineer-led rounds. The hiring manager is already sold on the business-side story; what's left is proving hands-on engineering depth to a senior engineer, the coding and system design rounds, and the CIO and Deputy CIO.

rows.v: Lindsey Mertz, Director of Revenue Operations, Upside (hiring manager; introduced themself as Director, the prep said Senior Director)
Staff Forward Deployed Engineer, GTM Platform. Same spec as Staff Full Stack Engineer, GTM Systems ('posted as 2 different titles')
Sits in GTM, not engineering. Reports to Lindsey, with dotted lines to other teams. Solo engineer at first.
Recruiter (Katie), then a senior engineer chat, then a vibe-coding assessment, then a system design panel, then the CIO and Deputy CIO. About 1 to 2 weeks in total.

items.html: Origin: a board member, the COO of Vercel, showed an agentic SDR stack (11 SDRs, 10 redeployed). Lindsey vibe-coded a prototype on Vercel, Supabase, Railway and RAG in 4 days.
Current build: Lindsey is building a bare-bones CRM with content management and self-service onboarding (customers sign agreements) 'on the side of my desk'.
Why now: the 2027 site and customer targets can't be met with an enterprise sales cycle, so they need to go downmarket.
Roadmap: master data management, then self-service for the long tail, then an agentic SDR, then a digital sales room (Gong and Clay context).
Salesforce: about $375K a year ('3 quarters of half a million'), 'bloated'. Lindsey wants the admins to work as quasi-product engineers.
Org: GTM under 100 people. The CIO/CTO drives R&D AI adoption; the president of GTM is involved.

blocks.h2: Exhibit 1 · Ex-Ante (from the Upside Interview Prep artifact)

fields.label: D · Question
fields.value: Does Upside's GTM Platform role fit, and do they see it?

fields.label: True north
fields.value: Leave with a named next step and the first workflow they'd want fixed.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: A sales ops leader will weigh workflow empathy and fast wins over engineering pedigree; the forward-deployed story lands if told in RevOps terms.

fields.label: Forks
fields.value: Strong: names a painful workflow, asks how you'd attack it, next round with a named panel. Mixed: probes staff-level depth or the commerce domain. Weak: wants a classic staff engineer.

p: Nine load-bearing claims went to an independent claims-skeptic (Sonnet) that read the whole transcript. It struck two of my reads and softened two more. The rulings are below; the struck ones are fixed in the Recoil tab.

rows: Lindsey asked about progressing; Katie call in a day or two

'would you be interested in progressing into further stages' and 'the two of you will probably have a conversation over the next day or two'. 'Advanced' is never said outright, but Zach's own read (promising, Lindsey wrote a lot down) agrees.
The req is real and funded
Same role under two titles and the 2027 target are grounded. Funding isn't: 'I didn't have budget for a ton of staff'. Team growth is 'my prediction'.
First build target named: CRM plus self-service onboarding
'a bare-bones CRM tied into a self-service platform'. Caveat: it's Lindsey's own build and the hire may rebuild it.
Empathy over pedigree only partly confirmed
'I need someone who has put in those 10,000 hours'; the loop is engineer-gated.
'trying to shut up' was about Lindsey making room for Zach's questions. Only the self-admitted long overview stands.
'I just don't know if that'd be the best use of my time or yours', next to 'I can manually review Python stuff'.
The 60-day number and the planned close weren't used
Neither appears anywhere in the transcript.
Best and worst case as stated
Best case: 'central focal point'. Worst case: single-purpose tool, 'probability of that is low'. No base case given.
'very well aligned with ... how I'm thinking about it' is partial fit evidence. Not proof of an offer.

rows.v: Strong / Mixed / Weak fork; empathy over pedigree
Strong on the hiring manager: workflow named, real interest, Lindsey wrote a lot down and barely pushed back (Zach's own read). Next step is the recruiter, and the full loop was described.
Strong, with a Mixed tail: the engineering-depth probe moves to the later rounds instead of this call
'I need an engineer. I need someone who has put in those 10,000 hours and thinks about extensibility.'
YELLOW, trending up. Not GREEN: the engineer rounds are untested.

items.html: Lindsey asked twice whether the role would really interest Zach ('feels a little different'). The doubt is that Zach is overqualified or a consultant, not that Zach can't do it.
Lindsey has never run this process before ('my first rodeo'), so Katie owns the format details.
Lindsey scanned the ARCS beliefs page live and called it 'fascinating'. The decision-ledger idea landed.
Lindsey uses Claude Code and the Vercel stack personally. Shared tooling is rapport.

rows.v: Posted JD with a $214K to $245K+ range, and the hiring manager was met. Budget isn't confirmed ('didn't have budget for a ton of staff'), and the final decision includes the CIO. 'it's actually the same role. It was posted as 2 different titles.'

items.html: Hand-coding reluctance said out loud. Reframe it before the senior engineer chat.
Long answers (the opening overview ran long). Keep engineer-round answers short.
Comp, level and office days (posting: Monday, Tuesday and Thursday in NYC) weren't discussed. Raise them with Katie.
Checked 2026-10-20: status.arcs.care and /beliefs contain no counterpart names or secrets. The pages aren't marked noindex, though.
BAR ruin edge: being judged unwilling to code in the vibe-coding round. Recoverable if the format allows AI tools; costly if it doesn't.
Loki: the cheapest way to break 'strong fit' is one senior engineer saying 'harness operator, not engineer'.
Bayesian: the hiring manager's prior went up. The loop's prior is held until Katie confirms the format.

blocks.h2: ATG pre-mortem: assume it's dead in 90 days
rows: Ask the band and level first. Bottleneck: the earliest node in your court.
Lead with hand-built specifics: schema, migrations, gates.
Format unknown; part may be without AI
Do a timed warmup on Coderbyte-style problems.
Use Lindsey's own scale point: no need to build to enterprise grade.
Governance, and GTM sitting outside engineering
Show controls, audit trails and no lock-in.
A narrow first tool, shipped within 60 days, outcomes captured inside existing work
Product owners who define 'done' and run acceptance tests; prototypes reviewed in Slack
A phased, headless move: back end first, then the front end, validated with user tests
Receipts, gates, and decisions written down for the next engineer

p: What survives if the format goes badly: Zach thinks in RevOps terms and in systems, and Lindsey already said so. The part that can still break is proof of hands-on coding, so that's where the prep goes.
